_note: Seventh batch, five entries: the drawn standard of the 1890s, the studio-made Vamp, the forces' voice, a parish for a footballer, and the address at Tepeyac. Facts were read this session from the full-text extracts fetched into episode/.chrome/b7src; no page was opened in a browser, so every record is retrievable with its URL and nothing here is upgraded to verified. Where the sources disagree - the Gibson Girl's 1890 debut against a caption reading 'created 1898' - the entry says so rather than picking silently. All five land verified:false.

entries.title: Trying to live up to the standard of his girls
entries.summary: A pen-and-ink standard of American womanhood, sold through the magazines and advertisements of the 1890s, that thousands of real women were documented trying to live up to - and that could never be disappointed, because it was never a person.
entries.significance: **She was a drawing, and the labour of living up to her was real.** The Gibson Girl - the character created by Charles Dana Gibson in the 1890s for advertisements, run through the magazines of the Gilded Age - had no body, no biography and no lines. In 1894 Life printed the sentence that gives this entry its title: a writer wondering whether Gibson knew 'there are thousands of American girls, from Oshkosh to Key West, who are trying to live up to the standard of his girls.' The direction of the traffic is the point. Ink specified a standard; the readers supplied the posture, the interior and the life. **Nothing she was said to want could ever be disconfirmed, which is what her shelf is for.** The test is whether the figure can be the author of its own behaviour, and a pen-and-ink figure cannot: she could not contradict the women who rearranged themselves around her, and she could not disappoint them either. The sources make the same point from the other side, and the honest entry keeps their disagreement. The popular legend says Gibson's wife, Irene Langhorne, and her sisters were the originals; the article on the character will allow only that she 'may have been the original model', while the article on Gibson says the legend is contrary to fact - 'The first Gibson Girl appeared in 1890, more than two years before Gibson met the Langhorne family.' The face the audience organised itself around was not a portrait of anyone in particular. **And the blank surface carried whatever its maker believed.** The same accounts connect the figure to Gibson's own views of the United States as a white nation and to his eugenicist ideology - the reminder that a surface with no interior is a perfect vehicle for the person holding the pen. The dating is left visibly imperfect rather than smoothed: one article commits to 1890 and carries a portrait caption reading 'created 1898'; the other will say only 'in the 1890s'. This entry takes the sentence that commits. The name outlived the fashion once, oddly: the SCR-578 survival radio carried by wartime aircraft was nicknamed the Gibson Girl for its shape. A standard drawn for magazines, adopted as a life, and finally a piece of equipment in a life raft.
entries.fits: Specified entirely by a pen and the pages that bought it: there is no interior anybody could get wrong, because there is no interior at all - the test's first half answers itself, and 'can it be the author of its own behaviour' is answered by the medium. That incapacity is the point of the attachment: a drawing cannot contradict the thousands of girls living up to it, cannot be caught failing, and cannot be disappointed by them either. Not a written character, who could at least talk back on the page.

sources.claim: The character created by Charles Dana Gibson in the 1890s for advertisements, spanning the late Gilded Age and Progressive Era; the 1894 Life line, 'there are thousands of American girls, from Oshkosh to Key West, who are trying to live up to the standard of his girls'; the connection drawn to Gibson's views of the United States as a white nation and his eugenicist ideology; Irene Langhorne 'may have been the original model'; the SCR-578 survival radio nickname.

Contrary to popular legend, Gibson's wife and her Langhorne sisters did not inspire the Gibson Girls: 'The first Gibson Girl appeared in 1890, more than two years before Gibson met the Langhorne family.' The same article carries a portrait caption reading 'Gibson Girl, created 1898', which the entry records as a disagreement rather than resolving it.

entries.title: Anagram of Arab death
entries.summary: A studio invented an Egyptian past for its newest star, told the press the invention was a hoax, and the audience kept the invention anyway - the Vamp, whose films are now mostly ash.
entries.significance: **The studio wrote her a past, and the past is what the audience bought.** Theda Bara was born Theodosia Burr Goodman in 1885; the Vamp was assembled at a press conference. When A Fool There Was opened in January 1915 - produced by William Fox, directed by Frank Powell, with Bara billed simply as 'The Vampire' - Fox gave the press an elaborate fictional biography making her an exotic Arabian actress, presented her in a flamboyant fur outfit, and then deliberately leaked that the whole thing was a hoax, which the film's record calls one of Hollywood's first publicity stunts. The invented origin ran further than the stunt: the star was said to be Egyptian-born, interested in the occult, the daughter of an Arab sheik and a French woman, born in the Sahara, and the name, per the studio's own account, was 'an anagram of Arab death'. **The distance was not a side effect of the star system; it was the product.** The film 'popularised the word vamp (short for vampire)', a femme fatale who fascinates and ruins the men she meets, and by her own quoted line - 'I will continue doing vampires as long as people sin.' - the arrangement had her consent. She was Fox's biggest star from 1915 to 1919, paid $4,000 a week at her peak, and made 43 films between 1914 and 1926 before marrying Charles Brabin in 1921 and retiring in 1926. **And almost nothing of what the audiences loved is left to check.** Complete prints of six of the 43 films survive; the 1937 Fox vault fire took most of the rest. So the object here is manufactured twice over - a real woman under a written biography, sold with a wink, and then mostly lost to fire. The record holds about six honest documents of what the crowds were actually watching, one of them A Fool There Was, entered into the National Film Registry in 2015. The rest of the relationship runs on press materials.
entries.fits: A publicity office assembled the figure the audience attached to, and the shelf expects exactly this case: 'if the work was assembled for them, they are still a persona but the manufacturing is the story.' The distance the shelf names is doubled here - a finished film cannot be caught changing, and a finished false biography never had to be revised, because the audience bought its terms up front. Not a fiction, which is the shelf's 'not': behind the Vamp there was a real woman, whose retirement simply stopped the printing.

sources.claim: Born Theodosia Burr Goodman, 29 July 1885 - 7 April 1955; Fox 'concocted a fictitious persona for her as an Egyptian-born woman interested in the occult'; the name recorded as 'an anagram of Arab death'; the promoted origins (an Arab sheik's and a French woman's daughter, born in the Sahara); 'I will continue doing vampires as long as people sin'; Fox's biggest star 1915-1919 at $4,000 a week; 43 films 1914-1926; complete prints of only six survive; married Charles Brabin 1921, retired 1926.

1915 silent drama produced by William Fox, directed by Frank Powell, starring Theda Bara as 'The Vampire'; controversial intertitles including 'Kiss me, my fool!'; 'popularised the word vamp (short for vampire)'; based on the 1909 Broadway play from Rudyard Kipling's poem 'The Vampire'; the January 1915 press conference, the fur outfit and the intentional leak that the biography was a hoax - 'one of Hollywood's first publicity stunts'; one of the few extant Bara films; selected for the National Film Registry in 2015.

entries.title: A letter in words and music
entries.summary: A radio programme addressed the men of the forces as a letter in words and music, and the voice behind it kept the address running for the rest of her life.
entries.significance: **An institution pointed a microphone at a nation at war and put one voice behind it.** Vera Lynn's wartime programme, Sincerely Yours, went out on 9 November 1941 at half past nine, and its opening line reads like a job description for this site's whole subject: a letter in words and music, to the men of the forces. The Oxford Dictionary of National Biography's summary is the flat one: 'Her reassuring voice and mastery of radio made her the forces' sweetheart in the Second World War - a connection she fostered with her ongoing commitment to veterans and memory of the war.' Everything in the tie was addressed to people she would never meet, on a schedule, by name of service. She was taken off the air after the broadcast of 22 March 1942 and stayed off for eighteen months; the successor programme, 'It's Time for Vera Lynn', began on 31 October 1943. **The work was finished before the audience arrived, which is the shelf's property.** 'We'll Meet Again' - written by Ross Parker and Hughie Charles - was first recorded on 28 September 1939, in the opening weeks of the war, by Lynn with Arthur Young; most of the people who would spend five years with the song had not yet been sent anywhere. A pressed recording cannot be caught changing and a broadcaster was never in the room, which is the distance this shelf describes. **And then the address outlived its occasion, which is the unusual part.** The commitment ran for decades after the war - the article records a Burma Star received in 1985 - and in 1953 she re-recorded the song with British Armed Forces personnel included on the recording. A 2000 poll made her the Briton who best exemplified the spirit of the 20th century; in 2009, at 92, she became the oldest living artist to top the UK album chart; and shortly before her death in June 2020 she addressed the country once more, ahead of the Queen's broadcast at the start of the pandemic. Broadcast bonds are not answered; the rare thing here is a near side that never stopped sending. Recorded in the first weeks of the war and played in a Cold War broadcast plan for use after a nuclear attack, the song kept being aimed at whoever was still listening.
entries.fits: The work was finished before the audience arrived - the song was recorded on 28 September 1939, and the forces who spent the war with it heard it in places she would never see, which is the shelf's distance in its literal form. There is a version of her that exists whether or not anyone is watching: pressed, broadcast, and still being sent long after the war it was sent to had ended, which is why the attachment survives the person. Not an athlete, whose tie moves with a role, and not an office: what was addressed was a voice and a body of work, on a schedule, for five years and then for the rest of her life.

sources.claim: Born 20 March 1917, died 18 June 2020; ODNB: 'Her reassuring voice and mastery of radio made her the forces' sweetheart in the Second World War - a connection she fostered with her ongoing commitment to veterans and memory of the war'; Sincerely Yours premiered 9 November 1941 at 21:30 with the greeting 'to the men of the forces - a letter in words and Music'; off air after the 22 March 1942 broadcast for eighteen months; 'It's Time for Vera Lynn' from 31 October 1943; the 1953 re-recording with British Armed Forces personnel; the 1985 Burma Star; the 2000 poll ('the Briton who best exemplified the spirit of the 20th century'); in 2009 she became the oldest living artist to top the UK album chart; the 2020 message ahead of the Queen's broadcast.

A 1939 song by Ross Parker and Hughie Charles; first recorded on 28 September 1939 by Vera Lynn with Arthur Young; later included in the BBC's Cold War plan for broadcasting after a nuclear attack (the Wartime Broadcasting Service); re-recorded in 1953.

entries.title: After Diego
entries.summary: A church founded in Rosario on Maradona's thirty-eighth birthday, with a calendar counted from him and a baptism performed with a football - the fan bond that wrote itself a liturgy while its god was still playing.
entries.significance: **They built a church out of a football player, and they date everything from him.** The Iglesia Maradoniana describes itself as a parody religion centred on Diego Maradona, and it was founded in Rosario, the city of his birth, on 30 October 1998 - his thirty-eighth birthday - by Héctor Campomar, Alejandro Verón and Hernán Amez. Its years are counted from his name: d. D., después de Diego, 'after Diego'; its god is written D10S, a joke across Dios and the ten on his shirt; and the phrase the sources record for what he is, in Argentina, is 'God of football'. **One founder said the whole subject out loud.** Verón's explanation: 'I have a rational religion and that's the Catholic Church and I have a religion passed on my heart and passion and that's Diego Maradona.' Nothing in the relation is reciprocal and nothing about it is a mistake - a real man was promoted into a position where the vocabulary of address already existed, and the vocabulary fit. The church kept the form of the thing it parodies: it baptises, and the record describes the rite as heading a football in front of an altered photograph associated with the 1986 Hand of God goal. **The member count is self-reported, and the entry keeps it that way.** The church claims more than 40,000 members worldwide, with over 9,000 in Spain; those are its own figures, reported as such. What needs no counting is the shape: a fan bond that built itself a liturgy, on a schedule, with witnesses, while its figure was still on the pitch. The athlete shelf watches for whether an attachment survives the person leaving, and Rosario answered the question in writing, on a birthday, years early.
entries.fits: The far end of the attachment is the player, and the shelf's question - does it survive the person leaving - has an unusually early answer here: the members opened a church with a calendar counted from his birthday while he was still playing. Nothing about the tie could be handed to a successor, which is the shelf's line between an athlete and a club; and he remains in motion, the athlete's defining property, since the god of this church is a man who could be watched live. Not an idol's finished oeuvre - the addressing continues, in the present tense, on the church's own schedule.

sources.claim: 'Parody religion centered around Diego Maradona'; founded 30 October 1998, Maradona's 38th birthday, in Rosario by Héctor Campomar, Alejandro Verón and Hernán Amez; Verón's quotation on a rational religion and a religion passed on the heart; d. D. (después de Diego, 'after Diego') and D10S; 'God of football'; the baptism rite of heading a football before an altered photograph associated with the 1986 Hand of God goal; a claim of more than 40,000 members worldwide and over 9,000 in Spain.

entries.title: Am I not here, I who am your mother?
entries.summary: Four apparitions to a Chichimec farmer and one to his uncle, a single Nahuatl sentence that gave the devotion its title, and a cloth image the Catholic world has organised itself around ever since.
entries.significance: **The entire relationship is address, and the founding story is one reply.** According to the Nican Mopohua, written in Nahuatl, the Virgin appeared four times to Juan Diego, a Chichimec peasant, and once to his uncle Juan Bernardino, beginning on the morning of 9 December 1531. She spoke to him in his own language - Nahuatl, the language of the former Aztec empire - and identified herself as the mother of the very true deity. The sign he was sent to gather was Castile roses, not native to Mexico, blooming out of season on the summit of Tepeyac Hill; he carried them in his tilma, the cloak that bears the image venerated ever since. And the sentence the devotion is built on is her answer to his worry: '¿No estoy yo aquí que soy tu madre?' - 'Am I not here, I who am your mother?' - which the record calls the most famous phrase of the apparitions, and which is inscribed above the main entrance to the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, on Tepeyac Hill in Mexico City, the most-visited Catholic shrine in the world and, the article says, the third most-visited sacred site. **The shelf's test is address rather than watching, with the other end understood to hear, and that is the whole cult - built on one reply that nobody but a single man is recorded to have received.** The evidence has been contested from the beginning. The 1556 inquiry records an attack on devotion to an image 'painted yesterday by the Indian Marcos'; Sahagún recorded his suspicion that it was 'a Satanic invention to cloak idolatry under the confusion of this name, Tonantzin' - 'They come from distant lands to this Tonantzin as in olden times'. Juan Diego himself is doubted: Zumárraga's own writings never mention him, the 1556 inquiry omits him, he appears in no document before the mid-17th century, and in 1996 the abbot of the Basilica was forced to resign after saying Juan Diego was 'a symbol, not a reality'. None of it stopped anything. In 1754 the Sacred Congregation of Rites confirmed the apparitions and the December 12 feast; Leo XIII granted the decree of canonical coronation in 1887, executed in 1895; and in 2002 Juan Diego was canonised as the first indigenous American saint. **The image's own history is a record of being handled, defended and examined.** In 1887-88 the ten-point crown painted on the Virgin's head disappeared - the change was noticed on 23 February 1888, and eventually a painter confessed on his deathbed that a clergyman had instructed him to remove it. In 1921 a bomb left under the tilma by an anti-Catholic secularist damaged the altar and left the image unharmed; the survival is called miraculous by devotees. In 1981, examining the cloth under infrared light, Philip Serna Callahan and Jody Brant Smith found no trace of sizing or sketching underneath the paint, and no explanation for the original parts of the image or their preservation. That is the honest shape of the whole entry: the most-visited shrine in the Catholic world rests on a Nahuatl text and a piece of cloth, and the address has been going up to both, undiminished, for five hundred years.
entries.fits: Addressed, never met: nobody in the record meets her, and the other end is understood to hear - the founding sentence of the devotion is her answer to a worried man. The shelf is for the terminal addressee, where silence is read as meaningful rather than as failure, and this silence carries one exception on the record: a reply in Nahuatl to a man who was never able to prove he heard it. What the archive holds in place of a conversation is a text, a cloth, a calendar and five centuries of witnesses.

sources.claim: Four Marian apparitions to Juan Diego and one to his uncle Juan Bernardino, beginning the morning of Saturday 9 December 1531; the Nican Mopohua written in Nahuatl; she spoke to him in Nahuatl and identified herself as 'mother of the very true deity'; '¿No estoy yo aquí que soy tu madre?' ('Am I not here, I who am your mother?') as the most famous phrase, inscribed above the Basilica's main entrance; Castile roses gathered from Tepeyac in the December cold; the tilma image; the shrine as the most-visited Catholic shrine and third most-visited sacred site; the 1556 inquiry and the charge the image was 'painted yesterday by the Indian Marcos'; Sahagún on Tonantzin; the transfer of the feast from 8 September to 12 December (Informaciones Jurídicas de 1666; confirmed by the Sacred Congregation of Rites in 1754); the 1887 canonical coronation decree and its 1895 execution; the crown's disappearance in 1887-88 and the painter's deathbed confession; the 1921 bomb; Callahan and Smith's 1981 infrared examination finding no sizing or sketching and no explanation for the original parts.

Juan Diego as a Chichimec peasant, living at Tlacopan at the time of the apparitions; the doubts: Zumárraga's writings never refer to him, the 1556 inquiry omits him, he is unmentioned in documentation before the mid-17th century, and in 1996 the abbot Guillermo Schulenburg was forced to resign after calling him 'a symbol, not a reality'; the 1883 conclusion of García Icazbalceta that Juan Diego had not existed; the Codex Escalada announced in 1995; beatified 1990 and canonised by John Paul II on 31 July 2002 as the first indigenous American saint.
